# Goals of the lab overall

---

The skills acquired in this lab class are crucial for bioinformatic tasks using molecular data, such as data analysis, scripting,
and working in high-performance computing (HPC) environments. My hope is that you don’t just type the commands into the terminal and
move on -- I would like you to ***think*** about what these commands are doing and start imagining how they could be useful in analyzing your own data.


## For your success in the lab
Each lab is inteded to be a reference point for you on various bioinformatic tasks.
To make the most of these labs, please treat them like a **personal resource**, so
adjust any specific commands accordingly.

---

# Lab Deep-dive

---

### Overview of today's lab
This lab provides an introduction to UNIX/Linux operating systems and the fundamentals of connecting to remote servers in the context of bioinformatics.
Throughout the labs, you will gain hands-on experience with essential *bash* commands, including file manipulation, and remote server access.

I strongly suggest asking questions today while the exercise is fresh in your mind (and while your classmates are around to help you!).

### Accessing the HPC at William & Mary
- [ ] Access William & Mary's HPC
- [ ] Make the first container on the HPC
- [ ] Install some software into that container

## W&M's HPC server
If you are using your own computer and want to *access the HPC from off-campus*,
then you will need to download the W&M VPN client. See this [vpn installation link](https://www.wm.edu/offices/it/services/network/vpn/)
for instructions. If you are connected to the W&M Wi-Fi you will not need to connect to the VPN.

Once you are conneced to the W&M VPN, or using the W&M Wi-Fi, you will need to
`ssh` into one of the sciclone's [subclusters](https://www.wm.edu/offices/it/services/researchcomputing/atwm/systemarchitecture/nodes/).
SciClone is comprised of many different servers (subclusters), each with their own unique set of resources
(i.e., high powered CPU's but low RAM). For most of the lab, we will be using *bora*.

If using your own computer and you run into issues accessing the HPC, ask me for help if needed!


### Overview of the UNIX operating system and directory structure
1.	The core structure of Unix directories follows a hierarchical tree-like organization.
The root directory serves as the top-level directory, and all other directories and files are organized beneath it
2.	When you first connect to the server, you will be in your home directory by default.
3.	Keep this structure in mind when you’re navigating through directories, especially once we start up/downloading data to your personal computers.
4.	If you ever get confused where you are you can return to the home directory using `cd`

## Connecting to `bora.sciclone.wm.edu`

For both PCs and Macs, I recommend using the terminal to access SciClone.

1. Open the Terminal software

2. Connect to the remote server using `ssh` with your username:

   ::: {.callout-note title="SSH into Bora"}
   In the code below, replace `wm-username` with your W&M username!
   ```bash
   ssh wm-username@bora.sciclone.wm.edu
   ```
   :::

   When you connect, you will be sitting in your `home directory` on the HPC!

---

## HPC Navigation
Moving around the HPC uses common UNIX commands (I will provide a link to a useful cheatsheet).

When you first log in, you are interacting the HPC's `head-node` (we will talk about this in class!).
Additionally, the location where you first "land" onto the HPC is ***not where you will work!***

Before we do too much, let's use some basic commands to see what is in our current folder, move around, and check where we are:

1. It may be kind of weird to think like this, but the parts of your laptop that you interact with
   really are just graphical representations of folders (directories).
   This is no different on the HPC! We can see the contents of this directory really easily.
   ```bash
   ls
   ```
2. You should see a couple big directories, including `scr10`, `scr20`, `scr30`. These are the "scratch"
   spaces, which is our playground!

   ::: {.callout-caution title="Storage Limitations"}
   **Do not** store files outside of `scr10` for this lab. Additionally, **do not** use `scr10` as
   a semi-permanent storage space! It is purged every few months, so please treat it like a
   shared kitchen and make sure we clean up after ourselves when we can!
   :::

3. Let's move into `scr10`, which is where we will do most of our work
   ```bash
   cd scr10
   ```
4. It can be easy to get lost on the HPC! Thankfully, we have the **best unix command ever**: `pwd`
   ```bash
   pwd
   ```

   ::: {.callout-note title="`pwd` is your Friend!"}
   The output of `pwd` is the PATH to your current location. Each `/` marks a different
   directory, so you can see ***exactly*** where you are.

   This is referred to as the *absolute* PATH, which is just like having *exact* GPS coordinates for where you are!
   :::

5. If you ever get lost, and this will happen, simply using `cd` will bring you back to your `home directory`
6. While we are here, let's make a folder the lab too
   ```bash
   mkdir Biol404L
   ```
7. Move into the new folder you made!

   ::: {.callout-tip title="In case you get stumped" collapse="true"}
   Use the `cd` command to move into your folder!
   ```bash
   cd Biol404L
   ```
   :::

8. Use `ls` and `pwd` to see what is inside this folder and where you are on the HPC!
9. Move back to your `home directory`

   ::: {.callout-tip title="In case you get stumped" collapse="true"}
   Use the `cd` by itself to move to your `home directory`!
   ```bash
   cd
   ```
   :::

10. Soon we will be done moving around for a little bit, just a few more to do!
 Let's move *directly* into our `Biol404L` directory, then use `pwd` to check!
    ```bash
    cd scr10/Biol404L
    pwd
    ```
You made it!

11. We can also move "backwards" to a less "nested" folder. We can use `..` to navigate
    back a directory **relative** to where we are. Let's try it out and see what it looks like!
    ```bash
    cd ..
    pwd
    ```

12. Move back into your `Biol404L` folder (see the prior commands/steps if you need help, before asking me or a neighbor)
13. Let's move "backwards" two times at once!
    ```bash
    cd ../..
    ```

    ::: {.callout-note title="Did you notice?" collapse='true'}
    To move back one directory, we use `..`. However, to move back **two** directories, we have to put a '/' in the middle!

    You can do this as many times as needed, although it can get confusing...
    :::
14. Where are you now? How would you check?
15. If you feel comfortable, make sure to move back into the Biol404L folder.
16. One last task before we continue! Make a new directory called `Slurm_Scripts` then move into it!

    ::: {.callout-tip title="In case you get stumped" collapse="true"}
    You can use the `mkdir` command!
    ```bash
    mkdir Slurm_Scripts
    cd Slurm_Scripts
    ```
    :::

Great! You are now on your way to becoming a UNIX navigation expert.

## Dealing with Containers
This next section will combine a fair bit of commands, which will become more familiar as you work in this lab.
You are **not expected** to be an expert right away!

### Loading Modules (Software)
The HPC has quite a lot of software already installed on it. This varies by with subclusters
you are working with (remember we are working on `bora`).

::: {.callout-note title="Want to see the available software" collapse='true'}
If you do, then run the following command:
```bash
module avail
```
:::

We do want to use containers in this lab. To do so, we will be using [Anaconda](https://www.anaconda.com/)
and [BioConda](https://bioconda.github.io/).

1. Load the `miniforge` module
   ```bash
   module load miniforge3/24.9.2-0
   ```
2. Let's see what modules are loaded already
   ```bash
   module avail
   ```
   ::: {.callout-note title="What do you see?" collapse='true'}
   You should notice that two pieces of software are highlighted!

   SLURM and Miniforge3!
   :::

3. Miniforge3 is our `Anaconda` software. However, it does not natively connect or know where to find
bioinformatic packages. Most of those are available through [BioConda](https://bioconda.github.io/).
4. We will follow the BioConda setup instructions for `Conda` that are found on their website.
   ```bash
   conda config --add channels bioconda
   conda config --add channels conda-forge
   conda config --set channel_priority strict
   ```

Now we are almost ready to install software! Woohoo!

It is worth noting that `conda` refers to their "containers" as environments. For our
purposes, this is the same thing, so do not be alarmed!

## Submitting HPC Jobs
In this part we will set up a job submission script. These are important to
understand as we will be using them throughout the lab course.

I have placed a template of one below (I will break down what each part means!):
```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=some-job-name
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH -t 1:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=8G

```

It is nice to keep your job submission scripts together, staying organized is KEY!

---

### Making our first job-submission-script

We will actually be submitting a job to make our container ***and*** install some software!
The easiest option is to use an existing text editor in the terminal, `pico`

1. Open a new file, `prep_conda_env.sh`, with `pico`
   Your screen should be empty!

2. Copy and paste the template for our job submission that was found in the last section
3. To "write" the file quickly (equivalent of saving), press `ctl`+`o` keys at the same time
and hit `enter`
4. Now, using your arrow keys, please replace `some-job-name` with `env-prep` and "write" the file again
5. Great, we are ready to add our command! We will create a new environment, called `sra_prep`.
In it we will install several pieces of software:
   - sra-tools: this makes it easy to download raw data from NCBI's SRA repository
   - ncbi-datasets-cli: makes it easy to access genomes from NCBI's GenBank and RefSeq
   - parallel-fastq-dump: speeds up the initial unpacking of SRA data
   - fastp: quality trimming tool (also provides lovely QC outputs!)

   Add the following to your script:
   ```bash
   conda create -n sra_prep ncbi-datasets-cli sra-tools parallel-fastq-dump fastp -y
   ```

   Make sure to save!

6. Check your script (below)

   ::: {.callout-tip title="Working Submission Script" collapse="true"}
   ```bash
   #!/bin/bash
   #SBATCH --job-name=some-job-name
   #SBATCH --nodes=1
   #SBATCH --ntasks=1
   #SBATCH -t 1:00:00
   #SBATCH --mem=8G

   conda create -n sra_prep ncbi-datasets-cli sra-tools fastp parallel-fastq-dump -y
   ```
   :::

7. Exit the `pico` editor with `ctl`+`x`

8. Submitting the job to run is incredibly easy! You will just use `sbatch`
   ```bash
   sbatch prep_conda_env.sh
   ```
9. Now we wait... You can track the progress in the queue!
   ```bash
   squeue --m
   ```
   Above will show ***only*** your jobs, whereas the code below will show ***all** the jobs
   ```bash
   squeue
   ```
10. Once this is finished, you will need to make one more container! Updating the
`prep_conda_env.sh` script, you will need to:
   - [ ] create a new container called `txpt_quant`
   - [ ] install `salmon`
   - [ ] install `star`

   Make sure this is run before we meet next!

11. Once your job is finished, activate your container!
    ```bash
    conda activate sra_prep
    ```
    If it works, you will see `(sra_prep)` on the left-hand side of the terminal!

12. Look at the `fastp` help message and all its options (so many)
    ```bash
    fastp -h
    ```

    Using `-h` with *most* tools will bring up usage information along with all
    their options. It is a ~~lazy~~ nice way to make to sure that the software is
    installed!

13. To exit the HPC, simply press `ctl`+`d` at the same time!
    You should see something like: `Connection to bora.sciclone.wm.edu closed.`

Disconnecting from the HPC is safe to do any time that a job is running or queued!

In fact, that is the advantage of the HPC! You can queue some work then do something
else (nap, eat some cookies, compose a bioinformatics sonnet, etc)

You made it! Huzzah!
